column1: # THE WORLD REGISTRY — the shared vocabulary, and the only copy of it.
# Explained for app developers in docs/WORLD-CONSTRAINTS.md. That page describes
# this file; this file defines the rules. If they disagree, the page is the bug.
# A "world" is a host slot an app can run in. Go (CLI + browser engine), Rust
# (the badge) and JS all need to name the same set, so the set lives here and
# each implementation is tested against it — the same arrangement as VECTORS.tsv,
# and for the same reason: a vocabulary that exists three times drifts.
# FORMAT: <id> <TAB> <name-profile> <TAB> <notes>
# `name-profile` is which filesystem rules apply (see VECTORS.tsv). A WORLD is a
# host slot; a PROFILE is a rule set. They are not the same axis — several worlds
# share the portable profile, which is the point of having one.
# THE TWO NON-WORLDS, and they are different in a way that matters
# `undefined`  Nobody said. The app declared no world and the host asked for
#              none. This is the DEFAULT and the common case: an app that runs
#              everywhere has no reason to name a world. Resolves to the portable
#              profile, which is the strictest, so the default is the safe one.
# `unknown`    A world was named, and THIS BUILD DOES NOT RECOGNISE IT. Not the
#              same as undefined: something was said and could not be understood.
#              It happens when an app or payload built against a newer registry
#              meets an older host — which the badge's payload region makes
#              routine, since payloads outlive the firmware that reads them.
#              FAIL CLOSED. An unrecognised world gets the portable profile (the
#              strictest available) and a host that was ASKED for that world must
#              refuse to run rather than substitute one. Guessing is how an app
#              written for a richer world silently loses its output.
undefined
column3: nobody declared a world; the default, and the strict one

column1: unknown
column3: declared but unrecognised — fail closed, do not substitute

column1: # The real worlds
# `native` and `browser` both run the Go engine, so they share an implementation
# and still differ as slots: one has a terminal and a real filesystem, the other
# has a DOM and OPFS.
native
column3: CLI / desktop; a terminal and a real filesystem

column1: browser
# The badge's two worlds are the same component and the same imports — they are
# not two WIT worlds (EMBEDDED-PLAN D10). They differ in what reaches a human,
# and `badge-minimal` is a SIMULATION of a device with only a status LED.
badge-normal
column3: RP2350 Tufty: shows the app's text; FAT over USB

column1: badge-minimal
column3: RP2350 Tufty: one status colour, no text; FAT over USB

column1: # THE BADGER 2350 — same tier, different hardware, and that is the point.
# It is RP2350, so the engine, the payload catalog and the control channel are
# unchanged. What differs is the SURFACE: e-ink rather than a backlit TFT, which
# is a genuine test of whether the capability model holds rather than a second
# copy of the badge.
# Two things it will make us answer, both of which today's model leaves open:
#   - `StatusOutlet` has NONE and COLOR. E-ink has no colour and no backlight, so
#     "how is it going" reaches a person as WORDS or not at all — a third outlet,
#     or an admission that status is a colour and this world has none.
#   - A partial refresh is hundreds of milliseconds and the panel HOLDS its image
#     with the power off. Every repaint in this firmware assumes neither.
# Listed now so the vocabulary is ready before the hardware is, and so the enum
# that mirrors this file gains it in one place.
badge-badger-normal
column3: RP2350 Badger: e-ink, shows the app's text; FAT over USB

column1: badge-badger-minimal
column3: RP2350 Badger: e-ink, status only; FAT over USB
